'''John David Jackson''' (January 19, 1925 – May 20, 2016) was a Canadian–American theoretical physicist. He was a professor at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] and a faculty senior scientist emeritus at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]].<ref name="Cahn"/><ref>{{cite web|author=John Jackson|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/lsj/obituary.aspx?n=john-david-jackson&pid=180073742&fhid=11048|title=John Jackson Obituary – Lansing, MI &#124; Lansing State Journal|publisher=Legacy.com|access-date=2019-06-22}}</ref>

Jackson was a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] and was well known for his work in nuclear and [[particle physics]],<ref name="NAS"/> as well as his [[Classical Electrodynamics (book)|widely used graduate text]] on [[classical electrodynamics]].<ref name=electro>{{cite book|author=Jackson, J. D.|year=1998|orig-year=1962|edition=3rd|title=Classical Electrodynamics|publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]]|location=New York|oclc=535998|isbn=978-0-471-30932-1}}</ref><ref name="Saslow">{{cite journal |last1=Saslow |first1=Wayne M. |title=Book review: Classical electrodynamics, by John David Jackson |journal=Foundations of Physics |date=1999 |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=133–135 |doi=10.1023/a:1018821305089|bibcode=1999FoPh...29..133S }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Born in [[London, Ontario]], Canada, Jackson attended the [[University of Western Ontario]], receiving a B.Sc. in honors physics and mathematics in 1946. He went on to graduate study at [[MIT]], where he worked under [[Victor Weisskopf]], completing his Ph.D. thesis in 1949.<ref name="Quigg">{{cite journal |last1=Quigg |first1=Chris |title=John David Jackson |journal=Physics Today |date=October 2016 |volume=69 |issue=10 |pages=68 |doi=10.1063/pt.3.3338 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2016PhT....69j..68Q }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Jackson, J. D.|author2=Blatt, J. M.|year=1950|title=The interpretation of low energy proton–proton scattering|journal=[[Reviews of Modern Physics]]|volume=22|issue=1|pages=77–118|doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.22.77|bibcode=1950RvMP...22...77J}}</ref>

==Academic career==
Jackson held academic appointments successively at [[McGill University]], thanks to [[Philip Russell Wallace]], a prominent Canadian theoretical physicist, (January 1950 – 1957); then the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] (1957–1967); and finally the [[University of California, Berkeley]] (1967–1995). At McGill, he was Assistant and Associate Professor of Mathematics; at Illinois and Berkeley, he was in the Physics Departments. At the latter, he held appointments on campus and at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]]. After retiring from teaching in 1993, he continued to be active at LBNL.<ref name="Quigg"/>

===McGill and Princeton===
At McGill in the 1950s, in addition to appreciable teaching, Jackson found time for research on atomic processes and nuclear reactions at intermediate energies and the beginnings of his book on classical electricity and magnetism.<ref name="Cahn"/>

While on leave at [[Princeton University]], he found a fruitful collaboration with [[Sam Treiman]] and H. W. Wyld on weak interactions, particularly the various observable decay correlations in allowed nuclear [[beta decay]] involving the electron's momentum,<ref name="Cahn"/> its spin, the neutrino's momentum, and the nuclear spin that provide information about [[parity (physics)|parity]] conservation or non-conservation and [[T-symmetry|time reversal]] conservation or not.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Jackson, J. D.|author2=Treiman, S. B.|author3=Wyld, H. W.|year=1957|title=Possible tests of time reversal invariance in beta decay|journal=[[Physical Review]]|volume=106|issue=3|pages=517–521|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.106.517|bibcode=1957PhRv..106..517J}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Jackson, J. D.|author2=Treiman, S. B.|author3=Wyld, H. W.|year=1957|title=Coulomb corrections in allowed beta transitions|journal=[[Nuclear Physics (journal)|Nuclear Physics]]|volume=4|pages=206–212|doi=10.1016/0029-5582(87)90019-8|bibcode=1957NucPh...4..206J}}</ref> He also published an early paper on the theoretical foundation for the then recently discovered [[muon-catalyzed fusion]] of hydrogen isotopes.<ref name="Cahn">{{cite journal |last1=Cahn |first1=Robert N. |title=J. David Jackson (January 19, 1925 – May 20, 2016): A Biographical Memoir |journal=Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science |date=21 September 2021 |volume=71 |issue=1 |pages=23–36 |doi=10.1146/annurev-nucl-021621-035759 |bibcode=2021ARNPS..71...23C |s2cid=239067925 |issn=0163-8998|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Alvarez|first1=L. W.|last2=Crawford|first2=F.|last3=Crawford|first3=J.|last4=Falk-Vairant|first4=P.|last5=Good|first5=M.|last6=Gow|first6=J.|last7=Rosenfeld|first7=A.|last8=Solmitz|first8=F.|display-authors=2|year=1957|title=Catalysis of nuclear reactions by µ-mesons|journal=[[Physical Review]]|volume=105|issue=3|pages=1127–1128|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.105.1127|bibcode=1957PhRv..105.1127A|s2cid=123886206 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Jackson, J. D.|year=1957|title=Catalysis of nuclear reactions between hydrogen isotopes by negative mu-mesons|journal=[[Physical Review]]|volume=106|issue=2|pages=330–339|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.106.330|bibcode=1957PhRv..106..330J}}</ref>

===Illinois (1957–1967) and CERN (1963–64)===
While at the University of Illinois (1957–1967) Jackson initially continued work on weak interactions as well as [[strange particle]] interactions at low energy with Wyld and others. On sabbatical leave at [[CERN]] in 1963–64, he collaborated with [[Kurt Gottfried]] on production and decay of unstable resonances in high-energy hadronic collisions.<ref name="Campbell">{{cite journal |last1=Campbell |first1=Allan |last2=Stahl |first2=Franklin W. |title=Alfred D. Hershey |journal=Annual Review of Genetics |date=December 1998 |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=1–6 |doi=10.1146/annurev.genet.32.1.1 |pmid=9928472 |language=en |issn=0066-4197|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Robert">{{cite journal
 |last        = Cahn
 |first       = Robert N.
 |year        = 2017
 |title       = J. David Jackson 1925–2016
 |journal     = [[Biographical Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences]]
 |volume      = 2017
 |page        = 1
 |pmid        = 
 |bibcode     = 2017BMNAS2017....1C
 |url         = https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/jackson-j-david.pdf
 |access-date = }}</ref><ref name="Cahn"/><ref>
{{cite journal|author1=Gottfried, K.|author2=Jackson, J. D.|year=1964|title=On the connection between production mechanism and decay of resonances at high energy|journal=[[Nuovo Cimento]]|volume=33|issue=2|pages=309–330|doi=10.1007/BF02750195|bibcode=1964NCim...33..309G|s2cid=121279157|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/345301}}</ref> They introduced the use of the [[density matrix]] to connect production mechanisms to the decay patterns and described the influence of competing processes ("absorption") on the reactions.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Gottfried, K.|author2=Jackson, J. D.|year=1964|title=Influence of absorption due to competing processes on peripheral reactions|journal=[[Nuovo Cimento]]|volume=34|issue=3|pages=735–752|doi=10.1007/BF02750013|bibcode=1964NCim...34..735G|s2cid=35362627|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/2221228}}</ref>

During this period Jackson lectured at three summer schools—on dispersion relations at the first Scottish Universities Summer School in Physics, 1960; on weak interactions at the Brandeis Summer Institute, 1962; and on particle and polarization decay distributions at the Summer School of [[Theoretical physics|Theoretical Physics]], [[Les Houches]], 1965.<ref name="snapshots"/><ref name="Cahn"/> He also published three books, one on [[particle physics]], based on lectures at the Canadian Summer School in Edmonton and Jasper, 1957;<ref>{{cite book|author=Jackson, J. D.|year=1958|title=The Physics of Elementary Particles|url=https://archive.org/details/physicsofelement0000jack|url-access=registration|publisher=[[Princeton University Press]]|lccn= 58013935|oclc=536207}}</ref> the second, a small book on mathematics for quantum mechanics (1962) and the third, also in 1962, the first edition of his text on classical electrodynamics.<ref name=electro/><ref name="snapshots">{{cite journal |last1=Jackson |first1=J. David |title=Snapshots of a Physicist's Life |journal=Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science |date=December 1999 |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=1–33 |doi=10.1146/annurev.nucl.49.1.1 |bibcode=1999ARNPS..49....1J |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/full/10.1146/annurev.nucl.49.1.1 |language=en |issn=0163-8998|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The book is notorious for the difficulty of its problems, and its tendency to treat non-obvious conclusions as self-evident. Jackson's high standards and admonitory vocabulary are the subject of an amusing memorial volume by his son Ian Jackson.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Jackson|first1=Ian|title=Mathein Pathein: a thesaurus of the idiolect of John David Jackson (1925–2016)|date=2016|publisher=Ian Jackson Books|location=Berkeley}}</ref>

===Berkeley===
Moving to Berkeley in 1967, Jackson taught on campus, both introductory courses for physicists and engineers and graduate courses in particle physics and quantum mechanics.  His lecture notes from the latter have been made into book.<ref name=qm>{{cite book|author=Jackson, J. D.|year=2023|title=J. David Jackson: A Course in Quantum Mechanics |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]]|location=New York|isbn=978-1-119-88038-7|editor-last1=Cahn|editor-first1=Robert N.}}</ref> He did his research at LBNL and served in administrative positions at both the campus (Chair, University of California, Berkeley (UCB) Physics Department, 1978–1981) and the lab (Head, LBNL Physics Division, January 1982 – June 1984). In the formative years of the ill-fated [[Superconducting Super Collider]] (SSC) project, he served as deputy director of operations of the SSC Central Design Group.<ref name="Quigg"/><ref name="Cahn"/>

In the 1960s and 1970s his research alone and with students focused in journal publications and conference papers on models of high energy processes, radiative and resolution corrections for resonances in [[electron–positron annihilation]], spin-flip [[synchrotron radiation]] and the polarization of electrons in a [[storage ring]], and, after November 1974, the spectroscopy of the charm–anticharm particles. In 1973, he lectured again at the [[Universities in Scotland#Scottish Universities Summer Schools in Physics|Scottish Universities Summer School in Physics]] (SUSSP), on hadronic interactions at high energies,<ref name="snapshots"/><ref name="Cahn"/> and in 1976 at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC) National Accelerator Laboratory's, SLAC Summer Institute (SSI), on charmonium spectroscopy.<ref name="Cahn"/><ref>{{cite journal|author=Jackson, J. D.|date=August 18, 1976|title=Lectures on the new particles|url=https://www.slac.stanford.edu/pubs/slacreports/reports03/slac-r-198.pdf|journal=SLAC Report|volume=198|pages=147–202|bibcode=1976slac.conf....2.}} LBL-5500</ref> In 1973–74 he ran the nascent theory group at [[Fermilab]] and co-edited the proceedings of the 1973 "Rochester" Conference.<ref name="snapshots"/>

In January 1977 Jackson began a 17-year stint as Editor of ''[[Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science]]''.<ref name="Cahn"/> In much of the 1980s he was involved with many others in the high-energy physics community in activities aimed at the next step up in accelerators. Then in 1983 he became active in the R&D for the SSC, and on the program advisory committee for the SSC Laboratory when it began in Texas in 1988.<ref>{{cite web |title=CURRICULUM VITAE JOHN DAVID JACKSON |url=https://www-theory.lbl.gov/jdj/web_CV.pdf |website=Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) |access-date=25 May 2023}}</ref>

==Retirement years==
Jackson retired from teaching in May 1995, but retained his connection with LBNL. In the 1990s and beyond his time was increasingly devoted to semi-historical talks and publications on a variety of topics, with a foray into refuting suggestions that cancer may be caused by environmental radiation stemming from ubiquitous electronics use.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Jackson, J. D.|year=1992|title=Are stray 60 Hz electromagnetic fields associated with the distribution and use of electric power a significant cause of cancer?|journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]|volume=89|issue=8|pages=3508–3510|doi=10.1073/pnas.89.8.3508|pmid=1565645|bibcode=1992PNAS...89.3508J|pmc=48897|doi-access=free}}</ref> This includes a continuing series of papers in the ''American Journal of Physics'' on diverse topics in electromagnetism, including rebuttals of mistaken ideas. History of physics publications include the historical roots of gauge invariance,<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Jackson, J. D.|author2=Okun, L. B.|year=2001|title=Historical roots of gauge invariance|journal=[[Reviews of Modern Physics]]|volume=73|issue=3|pages=663–680|doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.73.663|arxiv=hep-ph/0012061|bibcode=2001RvMP...73..663J|s2cid=8285663}}</ref> examples of the misattribution of discoveries in physics,<ref>{{cite journal|author=Jackson, J. D.|title=Examples of the zeroth theorem of the history of science|journal=[[American Journal of Physics]]|volume=76|issue=8|pages=704–719|year=2008|doi=10.1119/1.2904468|bibcode=2008AmJPh..76..704J|arxiv=0708.4249|s2cid=117774134}}</ref> and the editing of a sequel to R. T. Birge's history of the Berkeley Physics Department.<ref>{{cite book|author=Helmholz, A. C.|editor=Jackson, J. D.|year=2004|title=History of the Physics Department, University of California, Berkeley, 1950–1968|publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]], Department of Physics}} Contains more recent information in appendices.</ref>

His students include [[Hubert Reeves]]<ref name="Robert"/> [[Gordon L. Kane]],<ref>{{cite news |title=Gordon L. Kane |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/47087 |access-date=25 May 2023 |work=American Institute of Physics |date=16 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref> Robert N. Cahn (LBNL),<ref>{{cite web |title=Robert Cahn |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/46762 |website=American Institute of Physics |access-date=25 May 2023 |language=en |date=22 January 2022}}</ref> [[Richard D. Field]]  and [[Chris Quigg]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Physics Tree – J. David Jackson |url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=97927 |website=academictree.org |access-date=25 May 2023}}</ref>

==Memberships and honors==
Jackson was a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (elected in 1961),<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1961&unit_id=&institution=University+of+Illinois}}</ref> a Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and a Member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (elected in 1990).<ref name="NAS">{{cite web|title=J. David Jackson|website=National Academy of Sciences|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/john-david-jackson-j9prkn/}}</ref> In 1956, he was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gf.org/fellows/7168-john-david-jackson|title=John David Jackson|website=[[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130903145600/http://www.gf.org/fellows/7168-john-david-jackson|archive-date=2013-09-03}}</ref> In 1989, he received an Honorary D. Sc. from his alma mater, the [[University of Western Ontario]].<ref>{{cite web |title=In memoriam: John David Jackson |url=https://physics.uwo.ca/news_events/archive/2015_2016/in_memoriam_john_david_jackson.html |website=University of Western Ontario |access-date=25 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref> In 2009, in recognition of his own contributions to classroom teaching and his textbook, the [[American Association of Physics Teachers]] created the "J. D. Jackson Award for Excellence in Graduate Education", with the first award in February 2010 to [[Eugene D. Commins]].<ref>{{cite web |title=J.D. Jackson Excellence in Graduate Education Award - AAPT.org |url=https://www.aapt.org/programs/awards/jackson.cfm |website=American Association of Physics Teachers |access-date=25 May 2023}}</ref>
